meta.title: Breathing Numbers Navigator — Knowledge Map v0
meta.description: Evidence-traceable product specification for adults whose symptoms and obstructive sleep-breathing numbers do not appear to match. Review date: 2026-08-09. Educational design artifact; not individual medical advice.

claims.Atomic claim: Sleepiness, fatigue, insomnia, nonrestorative sleep, headache, and cognitive complaints are clinically important but nonspecific; they justify evaluation but do not by themselves establish obstructive sleep-disordered breathing.
claims.Use in product: Prevents symptom-to-diagnosis shortcuts.
claims.Caveat / counterevidence: Symptoms can still be severe and deserve evaluation.
claims.Allowed user-facing wording: Your symptoms are real, but these symptoms have more than one possible cause.
claims.Disallowed inference: You have OSA/UARS because you feel sleepy.

claims.Atomic claim: Questionnaires and prediction tools should not be used alone to diagnose adult OSA without objective sleep testing.
claims.Use in product: Requires report/test evidence before diagnostic interpretation.
claims.Caveat / counterevidence: Tools can support risk assessment and triage.
claims.Allowed user-facing wording: A symptom score can estimate risk; it cannot confirm or exclude OSA by itself.
claims.Disallowed inference: A questionnaire result confirms or rules out OSA.

claims.Atomic claim: ICSD-3 adult OSA criteria count predominantly obstructive apneas, hypopneas, and RERAs as obstructive respiratory events.
claims.Use in product: Supports an arousal-inclusive interpretation when the report actually includes RERAs.
claims.Caveat / counterevidence: The exact report denominator and event definitions still need verification.
claims.Allowed user-facing wording: Arousal-based obstructive events can count in the clinical OSA framework.
claims.Disallowed inference: Only apneas and oxygen drops can count toward OSA.

claims.Atomic claim: The RERA-predominant pattern historically called UARS is subsumed under OSA in ICSD-3 rather than retained as a separate diagnosis.
claims.Use in product: Avoids presenting UARS as a settled separate disease category.
claims.Caveat / counterevidence: Historical research labels remain useful for literature retrieval and phenotype description.
claims.Allowed user-facing wording: This pattern is often described historically as UARS; current classification places it within OSA.
claims.Disallowed inference: The app has diagnosed a separate disease called UARS.

claims.Atomic claim: The canonical historical UARS series described daytime sleepiness with inspiratory flow limitation and increasing respiratory effort terminating in brief arousals despite low conventional apnea/hypopnea burden.
claims.Use in product: Defines the historical phenotype without importing a modern cutoff.
claims.Caveat / counterevidence: Historical, small, uncontrolled, and sensor/scoring dependent.
claims.Allowed user-facing wording: Your findings may resemble the historical UARS pattern.
claims.Disallowed inference: The original study proves your symptoms are caused by UARS.

claims.Atomic claim: Published UARS definitions and numeric thresholds vary; no single universally validated rule lets a consumer app assign a stand-alone UARS diagnosis.
claims.Use in product: Creates an explicit unresolved-mechanism state.
claims.Evidence type: Historical literature + observational definitions + secondary review
claims.Caveat / counterevidence: Variation does not mean the underlying physiology is fictitious.
claims.Allowed user-facing wording: The report raises an arousal-based obstruction question that needs clinician interpretation.
claims.Disallowed inference: AHI below 5 plus symptoms automatically equals UARS.

claims.Atomic claim: Every respiratory index shown in the app must retain its study type, date, scoring rule, denominator, signal set, and treatment state.
claims.Use in product: Core provenance requirement for all metric objects.
claims.Caveat / counterevidence: Some reports omit one or more fields; preserve them as unknown.
claims.Allowed user-facing wording: This number is interpreted only with its test and scoring context.
claims.Disallowed inference: AHI values from different contexts are directly interchangeable.

claims.Atomic claim: Diagnostic PSG AHI is events per hour of sleep, whereas HSAT generally reports a respiratory event index using monitoring or recording time rather than EEG-defined total sleep time.
claims.Use in product: Prevents AHI/REI conflation.
claims.Caveat / counterevidence: Some modern HSAT technologies estimate sleep time; the device method must be known.
claims.Allowed user-facing wording: This home-test index may use monitoring time, not measured sleep time.
claims.Disallowed inference: REI and PSG AHI always use the same denominator.

claims.Atomic claim: A PAP device residual event index (AHI-flow) is not equivalent to a PSG AHI because device algorithms and available signals differ and PAP lacks EEG arousal scoring.
claims.Use in product: Separates treated-device data from diagnostic data.
claims.Caveat / counterevidence: Device data remain useful for longitudinal monitoring.
claims.Allowed user-facing wording: The device number is useful, but it is not the same measurement as a scored PSG AHI.
claims.Disallowed inference: A device AHI of 1 proves there were no sleep-disrupting breathing events.

claims.Atomic claim: Under AASM Scoring Manual Version 3, accredited sleep centers should report hypopneas associated with a 3% desaturation or arousal; a 4%-desaturation index may additionally be reported for payer use.
claims.Use in product: Sets current clinical-versus-payer context.
claims.Caveat / counterevidence: Check report date and lab accreditation; payer requirements remain separate.
claims.Allowed user-facing wording: The 3%-or-arousal index is the current AASM clinical score; the 4% score may be an additional payer score.
claims.Disallowed inference: The 4% score is the only clinically valid AHI.

claims.Atomic claim: The adult H3A hypopnea rule requires at least a 30% airflow reduction lasting at least 10 seconds plus either at least 3% desaturation or an arousal.
claims.Use in product: Defines the arousal-inclusive metric.
claims.Caveat / counterevidence: Use the exact scoring-manual version reported by the lab.
claims.Allowed user-facing wording: AHI-3A counts qualifying events linked to either a 3% oxygen drop or an arousal.
claims.Disallowed inference: Any flattened breath is an H3A hypopnea.

claims.Atomic claim: For current Medicare CPAP coverage policy, hypopnea is defined using at least a 30% airflow or movement reduction with at least 4% oxygen desaturation, and coverage thresholds are policy-specific.
claims.Use in product: Explains payer mismatch without calling it a diagnostic reversal.
claims.Caveat / counterevidence: Other payers and plans can differ; coverage is not medical truth.
claims.Allowed user-facing wording: The payer score uses a stricter oxygen-drop rule than the current AASM clinical score.
claims.Disallowed inference: A coverage denial means the clinical finding is false.

claims.Atomic claim: The same PSG can yield materially different AHI and severity classifications under different accepted hypopnea definitions.
claims.Use in product: Makes scoring-rule comparison a first-class pathway.
claims.Caveat / counterevidence: Magnitude varies by cohort and rule version.
claims.Allowed user-facing wording: Different scoring rules can move the same night across diagnostic thresholds.
claims.Disallowed inference: One score is fraudulent because another is higher.

claims.Atomic claim: When AHI-3A is at least 5 but AHI-4% is below 5, the discordance is consistent with OSA under the arousal-inclusive clinical rule and a possible payer threshold mismatch; it should not be automatically relabeled UARS.
claims.Use in product: Primary output for the PSG scoring-discrepancy pathway.
claims.Evidence type: Synthesis of classification, scoring, policy, and methods
claims.Caveat / counterevidence: Final diagnosis and coverage depend on symptoms, full study, clinician, and payer.
claims.Allowed user-facing wording: Your report crosses the clinical threshold under the 3%-or-arousal rule but not the 4% payer-oriented rule.
claims.Disallowed inference: This proves UARS rather than OSA.

claims.Atomic claim: The term RDI is used inconsistently across publications, laboratories, devices, and payer policy; the formula must be verified rather than inferred from the label.
claims.Use in product: Forces formula capture before RDI interpretation.
claims.Evidence type: AASM position + terminology audit + payer policy
claims.Caveat / counterevidence: A lab may clearly define RDI as apneas+hypopneas+RERAs per sleep hour; preserve that explicit definition.
claims.Allowed user-facing wording: Before interpreting RDI, check whether this report includes RERAs and which denominator it uses.
claims.Disallowed inference: Every RDI includes RERAs.

claims.Atomic claim: Most HSAT devices do not measure EEG arousals and therefore cannot score arousal-only hypopneas or RERAs in the same way as PSG.
claims.Use in product: Core blind-spot explanation after a negative or mild HSAT.
claims.Caveat / counterevidence: Some devices infer sleep or autonomic arousals; device-specific validation still matters.
claims.Allowed user-facing wording: This home test may not evaluate arousal-based breathing events.
claims.Disallowed inference: A negative HSAT rules out every form of obstructive sleep-disordered breathing.

claims.Atomic claim: If a single HSAT is negative, inconclusive, or technically inadequate in an adult with suspected OSA, PSG should be performed.
claims.Use in product: Routes negative/inconclusive HSAT to clinician discussion of PSG.
claims.Caveat / counterevidence: Urgency and modality depend on clinical context.
claims.Allowed user-facing wording: A negative or inadequate home test does not end the evaluation when suspicion remains; discuss in-lab PSG.
claims.Disallowed inference: Repeat home testing is always the required next step.

claims.Atomic claim: HSAT is recommended as a diagnostic option for uncomplicated adults who have signs and symptoms indicating increased risk of moderate-to-severe OSA.
claims.Use in product: Checks intended-use fit.
claims.Caveat / counterevidence: It is not a general screening tool for every sleep complaint.
claims.Allowed user-facing wording: Home testing is best validated for uncomplicated adults at increased risk of moderate-to-severe OSA.
claims.Disallowed inference: Any adult with fatigue is an appropriate HSAT candidate.

claims.Atomic claim: PSG is preferred over HSAT when significant cardiorespiratory disease, potential respiratory-muscle weakness, awake or suspected sleep hypoventilation, chronic opioid use, stroke history, or severe insomnia is present.
claims.Use in product: Adds a scope/safety gate before HSAT interpretation.
claims.Caveat / counterevidence: This is not an exhaustive emergency screen or individualized order.
claims.Allowed user-facing wording: These conditions can make in-lab PSG the preferred diagnostic test.
claims.Disallowed inference: The app can choose the test without clinician review.

claims.Atomic claim: When monitoring time exceeds true sleep time, an HSAT event index can underestimate the event frequency per hour of sleep.
claims.Use in product: Explains denominator dilution.
claims.Caveat / counterevidence: Not every HSAT overestimates sleep time; inspect device method and recording quality.
claims.Allowed user-facing wording: If you were awake for part of the recording, the index may be diluted.
claims.Disallowed inference: A low REI is definitely a false negative.

claims.Atomic claim: Technical adequacy and signal quality must be assessed before a negative or mild HSAT is treated as interpretable.
claims.Use in product: Requires adequacy state and missing-signal flag.
claims.Caveat / counterevidence: A report may call the test adequate even when individual channels have limitations; preserve both.
claims.Allowed user-facing wording: First confirm that the home test had adequate usable signals.
claims.Disallowed inference: Any missing signal automatically proves OSA.

claims.Atomic claim: Sleep-apnea event rates vary from night to night, and single-night testing can misclassify severity, with mild and moderate ranges especially vulnerable.
claims.Use in product: Adds measured uncertainty near thresholds.
claims.Caveat / counterevidence: Variability does not make all single-night studies useless.
claims.Allowed user-facing wording: A result near a cutoff may not represent every night.
claims.Disallowed inference: Three nights are always required for diagnosis.

claims.Atomic claim: When an initial PSG is negative but clinical suspicion for OSA remains, a second PSG may be considered.
claims.Use in product: Routes unresolved negative PSG to clinician discussion.
claims.Caveat / counterevidence: A second study is optional and individualized, not automatic.
claims.Allowed user-facing wording: If suspicion remains after a negative PSG, a clinician may consider repeat PSG.
claims.Disallowed inference: A second PSG is mandatory.

claims.Atomic claim: Total sleep time and REM/supine exposure help judge whether a study sampled the conditions in which obstruction may be most evident, but limited exposure alone does not mechanically invalidate the study.
claims.Use in product: Captures representativeness without deterministic rules.
claims.Caveat / counterevidence: Report interpretation requires the full hypnogram, position data, and clinical context.
claims.Allowed user-facing wording: Limited REM or back-sleeping time can reduce confidence in how representative the night was.
claims.Disallowed inference: No REM or supine sleep means the study is invalid.

claims.Atomic claim: PSG directly measures sleep stage and cortical arousals and records broader physiologic signals than most HSAT systems.
claims.Use in product: Explains why PSG can answer an arousal-based question.
claims.Caveat / counterevidence: Exact montage and scoring practice still matter.
claims.Allowed user-facing wording: An in-lab PSG can assess sleep and arousals that most home tests cannot.
claims.Disallowed inference: Every PSG automatically scores RERAs correctly.

claims.Atomic claim: A RERA is a sequence of breaths lasting at least 10 seconds with increasing respiratory effort or inspiratory flattening that leads to arousal and does not meet apnea or hypopnea criteria.
claims.Use in product: Defines the event only when the lab actually scored it.
claims.Caveat / counterevidence: Use the report's scoring-manual version; respiratory effort can be inferred by accepted signals.
claims.Allowed user-facing wording: RERAs are arousal-linked obstructive breathing events that fall short of apnea or hypopnea criteria.
claims.Disallowed inference: Any snore or flattened breath is a RERA.

claims.Atomic claim: If RERAs were not scored or reported, their burden is unknown rather than zero.
claims.Use in product: Missing-data rule for the low-AHI pathway.
claims.Caveat / counterevidence: The absence of reporting may reflect local practice, not evidence of presence.
claims.Allowed user-facing wording: This report does not tell us the RERA burden.
claims.Disallowed inference: RERAs are definitely present because they were not reported.

claims.Atomic claim: Under ICSD-3 criteria summarized by AASM, at least 5 predominantly obstructive events per sleep hour with qualifying symptoms/comorbidity, or at least 15 per hour regardless, can support adult OSA; the event count can include RERAs when RDI is defined that way.
claims.Use in product: Supports the low-AHI/high-RDI interpretation.
claims.Caveat / counterevidence: Diagnosis remains clinician-made and requires a technically valid study and clinical context.
claims.Allowed user-facing wording: A verified arousal-inclusive RDI can be clinically diagnostic even when AHI alone is below 5.
claims.Disallowed inference: RDI above 5 always proves OSA regardless of formula or symptoms.

claims.Atomic claim: RERA burden is not uniformly associated with sleepiness or cardiometabolic outcomes in general-population data, so causal interpretation must remain cautious.
claims.Use in product: Places counterevidence next to positive phenotype evidence.
claims.Caveat / counterevidence: General-population findings may not apply to symptom-selected patients, and arousal-based hypopneas may absorb some events.
claims.Allowed user-facing wording: RERAs can be clinically relevant, but their significance is not uniform across people.
claims.Disallowed inference: Any RERA count explains all symptoms.

claims.Atomic claim: Flattening of the nasal-pressure inspiratory contour can serve as a noninvasive surrogate for inspiratory flow limitation and elevated upper-airway resistance.
claims.Use in product: Allows evidence capture from PSG airflow shape.
claims.Caveat / counterevidence: Contour shape is a surrogate and depends on signal acquisition and processing.
claims.Allowed user-facing wording: Flattened nasal airflow can be a clue to increased upper-airway resistance.
claims.Disallowed inference: Flattening alone is a diagnosis.

claims.Atomic claim: Sensor hardware, sampling, filtering, signal scaling, and software can change the apparent airflow contour and therefore affect flow-limitation interpretation.
claims.Use in product: Requires device/signal provenance for waveform claims.
claims.Caveat / counterevidence: Visual expertise and validated algorithms can improve reliability but do not remove all uncertainty.
claims.Allowed user-facing wording: Waveform shape must be interpreted with the device and signal settings in mind.
claims.Disallowed inference: A screenshot is sufficient for definitive classification.

claims.Atomic claim: There is no single universally standardized isolated inspiratory-flow-limitation event definition or clinical threshold for consumer interpretation.
claims.Use in product: Prevents a threshold-based self-diagnosis feature.
claims.Caveat / counterevidence: Research methods can quantify flow limitation, but thresholds are method-specific.
claims.Allowed user-facing wording: Flow limitation is a graded signal that needs method and clinical context.
claims.Disallowed inference: More than a fixed percentage automatically proves disease.

claims.Atomic claim: Inspiratory flow limitation can occur in asymptomatic adults, so presence alone does not establish a symptomatic disorder.
claims.Use in product: Adds normal-range countercontext.
claims.Caveat / counterevidence: Higher burdens or symptom-selected contexts may differ; the study's 30% proposal is not universal.
claims.Allowed user-facing wording: Some flow limitation can occur without symptoms.
claims.Disallowed inference: Any flow limitation is abnormal and causal.

claims.Atomic claim: AHI does not quantify all flow-limited breathing, and measured flow-limitation frequency can vary partly independently of AHI.
claims.Use in product: Explains how low AHI and waveform findings can coexist.
claims.Caveat / counterevidence: Clinical thresholds and outcome prediction remain incomplete.
claims.Allowed user-facing wording: A low AHI does not describe every breath or every degree of airway narrowing.
claims.Disallowed inference: Flow limitation automatically explains symptoms when AHI is low.

claims.Atomic claim: Identified flow-limited events can be associated with arousal, oxygen desaturation, or heart-rate response, but a substantial subset has no immediate measured response; significance is context-dependent.
claims.Use in product: Uses balanced physiology language.
claims.Caveat / counterevidence: Immediate responses are not equivalent to long-term outcomes.
claims.Allowed user-facing wording: Some flow-limited events have measurable responses and others do not.
claims.Disallowed inference: Every flow-limited breath damages health.

claims.Atomic claim: PAP waveform flattening or a device flow-limitation flag should be treated as a hypothesis for qualified review, not as a consumer diagnosis or a basis for self-directed pressure changes.
claims.Use in product: Safety boundary for PAP data interpretation.
claims.Caveat / counterevidence: Clinicians may use waveform data within a broader titration and follow-up process.
claims.Allowed user-facing wording: This pattern is worth reviewing with a clinician; it is not a stand-alone diagnosis.
claims.Disallowed inference: Increase pressure until every flattened breath disappears.

claims.Atomic claim: PAP device usage duration is generally the most reliable component of tracking-system data.
claims.Use in product: Treats usage as a high-confidence input.
claims.Caveat / counterevidence: Clock errors, travel, naps, and multiple devices can still affect summaries.
claims.Allowed user-facing wording: Device-on time is usually reliable enough to compare with your sleep schedule.
claims.Disallowed inference: Usage proves treatment efficacy.

claims.Atomic claim: Therapeutic exposure should be compared with the user's full sleep opportunity and all sleep periods rather than inferred from an administrative adherence label alone.
claims.Use in product: Distinguishes coverage of sleep from policy compliance.
claims.Caveat / counterevidence: Exact sleep duration may be self-reported unless independently measured.
claims.Allowed user-facing wording: A good adherence label may still leave untreated sleep time if the mask is off for part of the night or for naps.
claims.Disallowed inference: Meeting an insurer threshold proves full-night treatment.

claims.Atomic claim: Residual-event and leak definitions differ among PAP manufacturers, limiting direct cross-device comparison.
claims.Use in product: Requires manufacturer/model provenance.
claims.Caveat / counterevidence: Within-device trends may still be useful.
claims.Allowed user-facing wording: Compare trends within the same device and keep the manufacturer's definitions attached.
claims.Disallowed inference: Leak and residual AHI mean exactly the same thing on every device.

claims.Atomic claim: Very high or very low device-reported residual event and leak values are generally more interpretable than intermediate values, whose clinical meaning is less certain.
claims.Use in product: Adds uncertainty bands rather than fixed universal cutoffs.
claims.Caveat / counterevidence: Even extreme values require clinical and device context.
claims.Allowed user-facing wording: Intermediate device values may need waveform, leak, and symptom context.
claims.Disallowed inference: A single intermediate value proves treatment failure.

claims.Atomic claim: Automated PAP algorithms can miss residual respiratory events, and qualified review of high-resolution flow data can add information.
claims.Use in product: Supports clinician waveform review when device data and symptoms conflict.
claims.Caveat / counterevidence: One retrospective study and device era; manual review is not a consumer diagnostic standard.
claims.Allowed user-facing wording: A low device AHI is reassuring but not infallible; waveform review can sometimes clarify.
claims.Disallowed inference: Every user should manually score their own PAP waveforms.

claims.Atomic claim: A higher baseline central apnea index predicted more residual events in one PAP waveform study, and persistent or increasing central events warrant clinician reevaluation rather than unsupervised pressure changes.
claims.Use in product: Routes central-event signals to a clinician safety branch.
claims.Caveat / counterevidence: Device central labels can be imperfect and etiology matters.
claims.Allowed user-facing wording: A rising central-event signal should be reviewed by a clinician.
claims.Disallowed inference: Treat central events by changing mode or pressure yourself.

claims.Atomic claim: Leak can complicate delivered therapy and the interpretation of device-reported residual events, so leak and mask/interface problems should be assessed before trusting a reassuring or alarming AHI-flow value.
claims.Use in product: Orders PAP review: exposure and leak before event interpretation.
claims.Evidence type: ATS official statement / product safety synthesis
claims.Caveat / counterevidence: Manufacturer leak metrics and thresholds differ.
claims.Allowed user-facing wording: Check mask leak and use coverage before drawing conclusions from the residual AHI.
claims.Disallowed inference: Any leak means the entire night was untreated.

claims.Atomic claim: Follow-up PSG or HSAT can be used to reassess adults with recurrent or persistent symptoms despite good PAP adherence.
claims.Use in product: Primary next-step output for persistent symptoms with apparently adequate PAP.
claims.Caveat / counterevidence: Choice of PSG versus HSAT depends on the question and clinical context.
claims.Allowed user-facing wording: Persistent symptoms despite good use can justify repeat sleep testing.
claims.Disallowed inference: A repeat study is mandatory or guarantees a new diagnosis.

claims.Atomic claim: Follow-up PSG may be used when PAP-generated data are unexplained.
claims.Use in product: Routes internally inconsistent device data to PSG discussion.
claims.Caveat / counterevidence: First confirm device, leak, and data-quality issues.
claims.Allowed user-facing wording: Unexplained device data are a recognized reason to discuss follow-up PSG.
claims.Disallowed inference: The device data alone diagnose a new sleep disorder.

claims.Atomic claim: PAP care should include adequate follow-up, troubleshooting, objective monitoring of efficacy and usage, and assessment of clinical response.
claims.Use in product: Defines the app's PAP checklist and handoff.
claims.Caveat / counterevidence: The app supports but does not replace clinician follow-up.
claims.Allowed user-facing wording: Good PAP follow-up combines the data with mask comfort, troubleshooting, and how you feel.
claims.Disallowed inference: A low AHI means follow-up is unnecessary.

claims.Atomic claim: Before labeling sleepiness as residual despite effective PAP, evaluate inadequate PAP, insufficient sleep, depression, sedating medications, other sleep disorders, and relevant medical causes.
claims.Use in product: Creates a parallel-cause checklist after respiratory data review.
claims.Population / scope: Adults with persistent sleepiness after CPAP
claims.Caveat / counterevidence: The list is not exhaustive and does not diagnose any alternative cause.
claims.Allowed user-facing wording: Breathing is one branch of the evaluation; sleep amount, mood, medications, other sleep disorders, and medical causes also matter.
claims.Disallowed inference: Persistent sleepiness proves residual obstruction.

claims.Atomic claim: Persistent sleepiness can remain despite apparently adequate OSA therapy and does not by itself prove residual upper-airway obstruction.
claims.Use in product: Prevents circular reasoning in the PAP pathway.
claims.Caveat / counterevidence: Residual sleepiness is a clinical problem that still deserves evaluation.
claims.Allowed user-facing wording: Ongoing sleepiness is important, but it does not identify the mechanism by itself.
claims.Disallowed inference: If you are still sleepy, PAP has failed.

claims.Atomic claim: Substantial daytime sleepiness together with a recent crash or near miss attributed to sleepiness, fatigue, or inattention indicates high driving risk and calls for immediate driving-safety counseling and expedited evaluation.
claims.Use in product: Global safety gate before all interpretation pathways.
claims.Caveat / counterevidence: Commercial-driver rules and local law require separate handling.
claims.Allowed user-facing wording: Do not drive while dangerously sleepy; arrange alternative transportation and seek prompt clinical evaluation.
claims.Disallowed inference: A specific legal clearance or universal emergency diagnosis.

claims.Atomic claim: Enhanced expiratory rebreathing space intentionally alters rebreathing and was studied with attended PSG and end-tidal CO2-guided specialist titration for PAP-associated respiratory instability; it is not a do-it-yourself UARS intervention.
claims.Use in product: Blocks unsafe rebreathing or mask-modification instructions.
claims.Caveat / counterevidence: Evidence is retrospective and not UARS-specific.
claims.Allowed user-facing wording: Do not modify rebreathing space or mask ventilation yourself; discuss the underlying problem with a sleep clinician.
claims.Disallowed inference: Instructions for DIY EERS or intentional CO2 rebreathing.

sources.Title: Clinical Practice Guideline for Diagnostic Testing for Adult Obstructive Sleep Apnea
sources.Authors / organization: Kapur VK; Auckley DH; Chowdhuri S; et al.
sources.Why it matters: Defines when HSAT is appropriate; directs PSG after a negative, inconclusive, or technically inadequate HSAT; lists conditions favoring PSG; allows consideration of a second PSG when suspicion remains.
sources.Key limitation: OSA diagnostic guideline, not a validation of a separate UARS diagnosis; recommendations apply within clinical judgment.

sources.Title: Polysomnography for Obstructive Sleep Apnea Should Include Arousal-Based Scoring
sources.Authors / organization: Malhotra RK; Kirsch DB; Kristo DA; et al.
sources.Population / setting: Adults evaluated for suspected or established OSA
sources.Why it matters: States that obstructive respiratory events include apneas, hypopneas, and RERAs; explains that classic RERA-predominant UARS is subsumed under OSA in ICSD-3; highlights the HSAT arousal blind spot.
sources.Key limitation: Position statement rather than an outcomes trial; payer rules can diverge.

sources.Title: AASM Scoring Manual 3: a step forward for advancing sleep care for patients with obstructive sleep apnea
sources.Authors / organization: Malhotra RK
sources.Design: Letter explaining Scoring Manual Version 3 implementation
sources.Why it matters: Explains that accredited centers should report hypopneas associated with a 3% desaturation or arousal and may additionally report 4%-desaturation hypopneas for payer use.
sources.Key limitation: Concise policy explanation; the full scoring manual is proprietary and versioned.

sources.Title: A transition to the American Academy of Sleep Medicine-recommended hypopnea definition in adults
sources.Authors / organization: Berry RB; Abreu AR; Krishnan V; Quan SF; Strollo PJ; Malhotra RK
sources.Why it matters: Defines the arousal-inclusive H3A rule and contrasts it with the H4 payer rule; discusses dual scoring and transition feasibility.
sources.Key limitation: Implementation paper, not a clinical-outcome comparison of every scoring strategy.

sources.Title: CMS National Coverage Determination 240.4: CPAP Therapy for Obstructive Sleep Apnea
sources.Authors / organization: Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services
sources.Population / setting: Adult Medicare beneficiaries seeking CPAP coverage
sources.Why it matters: Defines hypopnea for this coverage policy as at least 30% airflow or movement reduction with at least 4% desaturation and specifies AHI/RDI coverage thresholds.
sources.Key limitation: Coverage policy is not the same thing as the AASM clinical scoring rule; local and non-Medicare payer policies may differ.

sources.Title: The new AASM criteria for scoring hypopneas: impact on the apnea hypopnea index
sources.Authors / organization: Ruehland WR; Rochford PD; O'Donoghue FJ; et al.
sources.Why it matters: Demonstrates that accepted hypopnea definitions can materially change AHI and severity classification.
sources.Key limitation: Uses 2007-era scoring rules and is not UARS-specific.

sources.Title: Effect of Three Hypopnea Scoring Criteria on OSA Prevalence and Associated Comorbidities in the General Population
sources.Authors / organization: Hirotsu C; Haba-Rubio J; Andries D; et al.
sources.Design: Rescoring analysis in 2,162 home PSG participants
sources.Why it matters: Shows large prevalence and AHI differences across 1999, 4%-only, and 3%-or-arousal rules.
sources.Key limitation: Population associations do not determine the correct rule for an individual patient or payer.

sources.Title: Potential Underestimation of Sleep Apnea Severity by At-Home Kits: Rescoring In-Laboratory Polysomnography Without Sleep Staging
sources.Authors / organization: Bianchi MT; Goparaju B
sources.Why it matters: Shows how substituting time in bed for total sleep time can lower the apparent event rate and reclassify disease.
sources.Key limitation: Simulation of one HSAT limitation, not a head-to-head test of all devices.

sources.Title: Variability and Misclassification of Sleep Apnea Severity Based on Multi-Night Testing
sources.Authors / organization: Punjabi NM; Patil S; Crainiceanu C; Aurora RN
sources.Why it matters: Documents night-to-night variability and diagnostic/severity misclassification, especially around mild and moderate ranges.
sources.Key limitation: Portable monitoring and referral population; does not make every negative night invalid.

sources.Title: Treatment of Adult Obstructive Sleep Apnea with Positive Airway Pressure
sources.Authors / organization: Patil SP; Ayappa IA; Caples SM; Kimoff RJ; Patel SR; Harrod CG
sources.Population / setting: Adults with OSA treated with PAP
sources.Why it matters: Good-practice statement for adequate follow-up, troubleshooting, and objective monitoring of efficacy and usage after PAP initiation and during treatment.
sources.Key limitation: PAP treatment guideline, not a device-algorithm validation study.

sources.Title: Use of polysomnography and home sleep apnea tests for the longitudinal management of obstructive sleep apnea in adults
sources.Authors / organization: Caples SM; Anderson WM; Calero K; Howell M; Hashmi SD
sources.Population / setting: Adults with established OSA after diagnosis or treatment
sources.Why it matters: Allows follow-up PSG or HSAT for recurrent/persistent symptoms despite good PAP adherence and PSG for unexplained PAP-generated data.
sources.Key limitation: Guidance statements are not rigid rules; test choice depends on the clinical question.

sources.Title: Continuous Positive Airway Pressure Adherence Tracking Systems
sources.Authors / organization: Schwab RJ; Badr SM; Epstein LJ; et al.
sources.Venue: American Journal of Respiratory and Critical Care Medicine 188(5):613-620
sources.Why it matters: Finds usage tracking reliable but residual-event and leak definitions manufacturer-dependent; extremes are more interpretable than intermediate values.
sources.Key limitation: Device technology has evolved, but the provenance and standardization cautions remain relevant.

sources.Title: Residual Events during Use of CPAP: Prevalence, Predictors, and Detection Accuracy
sources.Authors / organization: Reiter J; Zleik B; Bazalakova M; Mehta P; Thomas RJ
sources.Why it matters: Automated PAP detection missed residual events in some patients; direct flow review improved detection; baseline central apnea index predicted residual burden.
sources.Key limitation: Single-device-era retrospective study; manual waveform review requires expertise.

sources.Title: Treatment of central sleep apnea in adults: an American Academy of Sleep Medicine clinical practice guideline
sources.Authors / organization: Badr MS; et al.
sources.Why it matters: Emphasizes individualized management and reevaluation of persistent central events and underlying risk factors.
sources.Key limitation: Central sleep apnea guideline; device flags are not a diagnosis and treatment depends on etiology.

sources.Title: Investigation and management of residual sleepiness in CPAP-treated patients with obstructive sleep apnoea: the European view
sources.Authors / organization: Craig S; Pépin JL; Randerath W; et al.
sources.Population / setting: Adults with OSA and persistent sleepiness after CPAP
sources.Why it matters: Structures evaluation of PAP factors, insufficient sleep, depression, medications, other sleep disorders, and medical causes before labeling residual sleepiness.
sources.Key limitation: Narrative expert review; individual workup and regional practices vary.

sources.Title: Sleep Apnea, Sleepiness, and Driving Risk in Noncommercial Drivers
sources.Authors / organization: Strohl KP; Brown DB; Collop N; et al.
sources.Venue: American Journal of Respiratory and Critical Care Medicine 187(11):1259-1266
sources.Population / setting: Noncommercial adult drivers with suspected or confirmed OSA
sources.Why it matters: Defines high-risk driving using substantial sleepiness plus a recent crash or near miss and recommends immediate safety counseling and expedited evaluation.
sources.Key limitation: Not a general emergency triage guideline and does not cover commercial-driver regulations.

sources.Title: A cause of excessive daytime sleepiness. The upper airway resistance syndrome
sources.Authors / organization: Guilleminault C; Stoohs R; Clerk A; Cetel M; Maistros P
sources.Design: Selected case series with experimental CPAP, n=15
sources.Population / setting: Sleepy adults with low conventional apnea/hypopnea burden
sources.Why it matters: Canonical description of sleepiness, inspiratory flow limitation, increased esophageal-pressure effort, and brief arousals despite low conventional AHI.
sources.Key limitation: Small, selected, uncontrolled, historical scoring and sensors.

sources.Title: Detection of flow limitation with a nasal cannula/pressure transducer system
sources.Authors / organization: Hosselet JJ; Norman RG; Ayappa I; Rapoport DM
sources.Venue: American Journal of Respiratory and Critical Care Medicine 157(5):1461-1467
sources.Why it matters: Validates nasal-pressure inspiratory contour flattening against elevated upper-airway resistance.
sources.Key limitation: Small sample; detecting flow limitation does not establish symptom causality.

sources.Title: Detection of upper airway resistance syndrome using a nasal cannula/pressure transducer
sources.Authors / organization: Epstein MD; Chicoine SA; Hanumara RC
sources.Why it matters: Shows nasal pressure detected more respiratory arousals than thermistor-based airflow, especially in UARS/primary-snoring groups.
sources.Key limitation: Small single-center study using historical case definitions.

sources.Title: Noninvasive Identification of Inspiratory Flow Limitation in Sleep Studies
sources.Authors / organization: American Thoracic Society workshop participants
sources.Venue: Annals of the American Thoracic Society
sources.Why it matters: Explains signal-shape methods, effects of hardware/software/filtering, and the need for standardized automated approaches and validation.
sources.Key limitation: Consensus and research-priority report; does not create a universal clinical cutoff.

sources.Title: Inspiratory Flow Limitation in a Normal Population of Adults in São Paulo, Brazil
sources.Authors / organization: Palombini LO; Tufik S; Rapoport DM; et al.
sources.Population / setting: Asymptomatic healthy subgroup from a 1,042-person cohort
sources.Why it matters: Shows that some inspiratory flow limitation occurs in asymptomatic adults; only 5% had more than 30% of sleep time affected under the study method.
sources.Key limitation: One manual scoring approach and threshold proposal; not a universal diagnostic standard.

sources.Title: Frequency of flow limitation using airflow shape
sources.Authors / organization: Mann DL; Georgeson T; Landry SA; et al.
sources.Design: Automated method development, 117,871 breaths from n=40
sources.Why it matters: Quantifies breath-level flow-limitation certainty and shows that flow-limitation frequency can vary partly independently of AHI.
sources.Key limitation: Small method-development cohort; no validated clinical UARS cutoff.

sources.Title: Immediate Physiological Responses to Inspiratory Flow Limited Events in Mild Obstructive Sleep Apnea
sources.Authors / organization: Guevarra JT; Castillo B; Joshi H; et al.
sources.Venue: Annals of the American Thoracic Society 19(1):99-108
sources.Design: Manual event scoring and physiologic-response study, n=58
sources.Why it matters: Shows variable arousal, desaturation, and heart-rate responses to identified flow-limited events and notes that an isolated IFL event lacks a standard definition.
sources.Key limitation: Mild-OSA sample and research scoring; immediate physiology does not establish long-term outcome thresholds.

sources.Title: Prevalence and Clinical Significance of Respiratory Effort-Related Arousals in the General Population
sources.Authors / organization: Ogna A; Tobback N; Andries D; et al.
sources.Why it matters: Provides counterevidence: predominantly RERA-based SDB was uncommon and RERAs were not associated with measured sleepiness or cardiometabolic outcomes under that study's criteria.
sources.Key limitation: Older population and arousal-inclusive hypopnea scoring may absorb events otherwise labeled RERAs; not equivalent to symptom-selected UARS.

sources.Title: Frequency and accuracy of 'RERA' and 'RDI' terms in the Journal of Clinical Sleep Medicine from 2006 through 2012
sources.Authors / organization: Krakow B; Krakow J; Ulibarri VA; McIver ND
sources.Why it matters: Documents inconsistent mention of RERAs and calculation of RDI.
sources.Key limitation: Journal-specific terminology audit, not a patient-outcome study.

sources.Title: Effects of Oral Appliances on Snoring and the Upper Airway Resistance Syndrome
sources.Authors / organization: In: Management of Obstructive Sleep Apnea
sources.Why it matters: Confirms that a modern OSA text treats UARS briefly and points mainly to a small oral-appliance research program.
sources.Key limitation: Very short secondary source; does not materially expand the primary evidence base.

sources.Title: Treatment of positive airway pressure treatment-associated respiratory instability with enhanced expiratory rebreathing space
sources.Authors / organization: Gilmartin GS; McGeehan B; Vigneault K; et al.
sources.Population / setting: CPAP-refractory patients with PAP-associated respiratory instability
sources.Why it matters: Original EERS evidence used attended PSG and end-tidal CO2-guided titration for ventilatory instability.
sources.Key limitation: Not a UARS treatment trial; intentionally changes rebreathing and does not support unsupervised modification.

sources.Title: Quality of life in upper airway resistance syndrome
sources.Authors / organization: Vizcarra-Escobar D; Duque KR; Barbagelata-Agüero F; Vizcarra JA
sources.Design: Retrospective referral cohort and population comparator
sources.Why it matters: Shows clinically important quality-of-life burden under one explicit UARS definition.
sources.Key limitation: Retrospective referral selection, definition-sensitive groups, and residual confounding.

nodes.Label: Begin mismatch review
nodes.User-facing prompt / message: We will first check immediate safety, then identify which kind of breathing number you have.
nodes.Missing-data behavior: Create a draft case.

nodes.Label: Drowsy-driving screen
nodes.User-facing prompt / message: Have you had substantial sleepiness while driving, or a recent crash or near miss you think was related to sleepiness, fatigue, or inattention?
nodes.Logic / evaluation: High risk if substantial sleepiness plus near_miss or crash.
nodes.Missing-data behavior: If unknown, show caution and allow continuation.

nodes.Label: Immediate driving-safety message
nodes.User-facing prompt / message: Do not drive while dangerously sleepy. Arrange another way to travel and seek prompt clinical evaluation. This app cannot clear you to drive.
nodes.Missing-data behavior: Always render when trigger is met.
nodes.UX notes: Keep visible; user may continue only after acknowledgement.

nodes.Label: Adult and jurisdiction check
nodes.User-facing prompt / message: Is this review for an adult, and are you using US clinical/payer context?
nodes.Logic / evaluation: Adult US continues full workflow; other states receive scope-limited education.
nodes.Missing-data behavior: Unknown age -> ask; unknown country -> omit payer-specific language.

nodes.Label: Symptom summary
nodes.User-facing prompt / message: Which symptoms are still affecting you, how severe are they, and did they change after treatment?
nodes.Logic / evaluation: Capture without mapping symptoms to a diagnosis.
nodes.Missing-data behavior: Allow 'not sure' and free-text other.
nodes.UX notes: Explain that symptoms and questionnaires guide questions, not diagnosis.

nodes.Label: Choose data pathway
nodes.User-facing prompt / message: Which result feels mismatched: a home test, an in-lab diagnostic study, or PAP data while on treatment?
nodes.Logic / evaluation: Route by available data and user goal.
nodes.Missing-data behavior: Unknown routes to report-acquisition node.

nodes.Label: Obtain the complete report
nodes.User-facing prompt / message: A complete interpretation needs the report's metric definitions, scoring rule, durations, and technical notes. Ask the testing center or clinician for the full signed report.
nodes.Logic / evaluation: Render when minimum metric passport is incomplete.
nodes.Missing-data behavior: Do not force guesses; save draft.

nodes.Label: Parallel symptom review
nodes.User-facing prompt / message: Breathing data are only one branch. A clinician may also review sleep amount, insomnia, circadian timing, medications/substances, mood, other sleep disorders, and medical causes.
nodes.Logic / evaluation: Append when symptoms persist or respiratory explanation is incomplete.
nodes.Missing-data behavior: Show even if respiratory findings are also present.

nodes.Label: Generate visit brief
nodes.User-facing prompt / message: Create a concise summary of what was measured, what the current data support, what remains unknown, and the top questions for the next visit.
nodes.Logic / evaluation: Render approved output templates with claim trace.
nodes.Missing-data behavior: Incomplete fields appear as 'not reported.'
nodes.UX notes: Never output a diagnosis or treatment setting.

nodes.Label: Identify the home test
nodes.User-facing prompt / message: Enter the device/test type, date, reported index name, recording or monitoring time, and any stated hypopnea/desaturation rule.
nodes.Missing-data behavior: Unknown fields remain explicit.

nodes.Label: Classify reported result
nodes.User-facing prompt / message: How did the report classify the test?
nodes.Logic / evaluation: negative, mild, moderate_severe, inconclusive, or unknown.
nodes.Missing-data behavior: If classification and number conflict, flag unexplained report.
nodes.UX notes: Do not recompute diagnosis from one number.

nodes.Label: Check technical adequacy
nodes.User-facing prompt / message: Did the report call the study technically adequate, and were airflow, effort, and oximetry signals usable?
nodes.Missing-data behavior: Unknown is not adequate.
nodes.UX notes: Explain each required signal in plain language.

nodes.Label: Check denominator and rule
nodes.User-facing prompt / message: Was the index divided by monitoring/recording time or estimated sleep, and did the rule require a 3% or 4% oxygen drop?
nodes.Missing-data behavior: Unknown denominator blocks direct PSG comparison.

nodes.Label: Check HSAT intended-use fit
nodes.User-facing prompt / message: Are any conditions present that can make in-lab PSG preferable, such as major heart/lung disease, neuromuscular weakness, hypoventilation concern, chronic opioids, stroke, or severe insomnia?
nodes.Missing-data behavior: If unknown, advise clinician review of test choice.
nodes.UX notes: Do not ask for detailed diagnoses beyond yes/no/unknown.

nodes.Label: Assess unresolved suspicion
nodes.User-facing prompt / message: Are important symptoms still present, or did a clinician remain concerned despite the result?
nodes.Logic / evaluation: Persistent symptoms/suspicion after negative or mild HSAT -> unresolved.
nodes.Missing-data behavior: Symptoms alone do not set diagnosis.

nodes.Label: PSG discussion indicated
nodes.User-facing prompt / message: A negative, inconclusive, or technically inadequate HSAT does not finish the evaluation when OSA is still suspected. Discuss in-lab PSG with your clinician.
nodes.Missing-data behavior: Show exact trigger(s).
nodes.UX notes: Avoid saying PSG will be positive.

nodes.Label: Arousal blind spot
nodes.User-facing prompt / message: Most home tests cannot directly score EEG arousals or RERAs, so this result may not answer an arousal-based breathing question.
nodes.Missing-data behavior: If device claims arousal/sleep inference, mark device-specific evidence needed.
nodes.UX notes: Do not call the HSAT wrong.

nodes.Label: Possible denominator dilution
nodes.User-facing prompt / message: If monitoring time included substantial wake, the event rate per monitoring hour may be lower than a sleep-hour rate.
nodes.Logic / evaluation: Set denominator_uncertainty when wake inclusion is plausible.
nodes.Missing-data behavior: No assumption if sleep/wake estimate is unavailable.

nodes.Label: Single-night variability
nodes.User-facing prompt / message: A result near a diagnostic boundary may not represent every night, particularly in mild or moderate ranges.
nodes.Logic / evaluation: Set variability_note when one night and near threshold.
nodes.Missing-data behavior: Do not require multi-night testing.

nodes.Label: Positive HSAT in intended-use setting
nodes.User-facing prompt / message: The home test may adequately identify conventional moderate-to-severe OSA in the setting for which HSAT is best validated, but persistent symptoms still require treatment-response and parallel-cause review.
nodes.Logic / evaluation: Preserve positive result and route to clinician follow-up.
nodes.Missing-data behavior: Do not reinterpret treatment need.

nodes.Label: HSAT report incomplete
nodes.User-facing prompt / message: The current entries are not enough to know what the home-test number means. Obtain the complete signed report and device/test details.
nodes.Missing-data behavior: Never infer scoring rule or RDI formula.

nodes.Label: Complete HSAT interpretation
nodes.User-facing prompt / message: Summarize capability, data quality, denominator, test-fit, and next-step states.
nodes.Logic / evaluation: Select approved outputs and route to global handoff.
nodes.Missing-data behavior: List unknowns explicitly.
nodes.UX notes: Prioritize no more than three questions.

nodes.Label: Enter diagnostic PSG metrics
nodes.User-facing prompt / message: Enter AHI-3A, AHI-4%, RDI, RERA index, arousal index, total sleep time, REM/supine exposure, oxygen data, and technical notes exactly as reported.
nodes.Missing-data behavior: Every field has 'not reported.'
nodes.UX notes: Do not ask users to calculate RDI.

nodes.Label: Identify scoring rule
nodes.User-facing prompt / message: Does the report name the hypopnea rule or provide separate 3%-or-arousal and 4% AHIs?
nodes.Logic / evaluation: Known dual, known single, or unknown.
nodes.Missing-data behavior: Unknown triggers missing-rule explanation, not a guessed label.

nodes.Label: PSG report definitions needed
nodes.User-facing prompt / message: Ask for the full report or lab clarification of the hypopnea rule, whether RERAs were scored, and how RDI was calculated.
nodes.Missing-data behavior: Continue with provisional, clearly labeled interpretation if user chooses.
nodes.UX notes: Do not block all educational content.

nodes.Label: Check for dual AHI values
nodes.User-facing prompt / message: Are both AHI-3A and AHI-4% available from the same study?
nodes.Logic / evaluation: Dual values must share study_id and denominator.
nodes.Missing-data behavior: If dates/studies differ, do not compare directly.

nodes.Label: Evaluate scoring discordance
nodes.User-facing prompt / message: Does AHI-3A meet at least 5 events/hour while AHI-4% is below 5?
nodes.Logic / evaluation: True only for compatible same-study metrics.
nodes.Missing-data behavior: If one score missing, state cannot assess.

nodes.Label: Clinical-versus-payer scoring mismatch
nodes.User-facing prompt / message: This same night crosses the clinical threshold under the 3%-or-arousal rule but not the 4%-only rule. That is a scoring and possible coverage mismatch, not automatic evidence of a separate UARS diagnosis.
nodes.Missing-data behavior: Omit CMS language outside US or if payer unknown.
nodes.UX notes: Display both metric passports side by side.

nodes.Label: Check clinical AHI range
nodes.User-facing prompt / message: Is the arousal-inclusive AHI, or the only explicitly clinical AHI, at least 5?
nodes.Logic / evaluation: If yes, preserve report/clinical OSA pathway; if below 5, inspect RDI/RERAs.
nodes.Missing-data behavior: Unknown scoring rule lowers confidence.
nodes.UX notes: Do not reclassify a clinician diagnosis.

nodes.Label: Check RDI and RERA availability
nodes.User-facing prompt / message: Are RDI and RERA index reported?
nodes.Missing-data behavior: Zero is accepted only if report says RERAs were scored.

nodes.Label: Verify the RDI formula
nodes.User-facing prompt / message: Does this report define RDI as apneas plus hypopneas plus RERAs per hour of sleep?
nodes.Missing-data behavior: Unknown formula blocks threshold interpretation.
nodes.UX notes: Quote exact report definition where available.

nodes.Label: Arousal-based obstructive event burden
nodes.User-facing prompt / message: A verified arousal-inclusive RDI can support the current OSA framework even when AHI alone is below 5, if the clinical criteria are met. Historically, this pattern was often called UARS.
nodes.Logic / evaluation: Set state=arousal_based_obstruction_supported when criteria inputs are present.
nodes.Missing-data behavior: Diagnosis remains clinician-made; show criteria inputs and unknowns.
nodes.UX notes: Lead with current OSA framing, then historical label.

nodes.Label: RERA burden unknown
nodes.User-facing prompt / message: Because RERAs were not scored, not reported, or the RDI formula is unclear, this study cannot tell us whether arousal-based obstructive events were present at a clinically meaningful rate.
nodes.Missing-data behavior: Do not infer presence.

nodes.Label: Check flow-limitation evidence
nodes.User-facing prompt / message: Did the report quantify inspiratory flow limitation or describe persistent nasal-pressure flattening?
nodes.Missing-data behavior: Unscored waveform impressions are lower confidence.

nodes.Label: Check flow-signal context
nodes.User-facing prompt / message: Was nasal pressure used, and are the acquisition method, filtering, and scoring approach described well enough to interpret the contour?
nodes.Missing-data behavior: Unknown context caps conclusion at 'possible clue.'
nodes.UX notes: Avoid requiring technical fields users cannot access.

nodes.Label: Flow limitation is a clue, not a diagnosis
nodes.User-facing prompt / message: Flow-limited breathing can coexist with a low AHI, but it is method-dependent, can occur in asymptomatic people, and has no universal consumer cutoff. Use it as a clinician-review clue.
nodes.Missing-data behavior: Show counterevidence and method caveat.
nodes.UX notes: Never label disease from percentage alone.

nodes.Label: Assess night representativeness
nodes.User-facing prompt / message: How much total sleep, REM sleep, and supine sleep were recorded, and did the report note unusual sleep or signal limitations?
nodes.Logic / evaluation: Create graded representativeness state; no hard invalidity cutoff.
nodes.Missing-data behavior: Missing values -> unknown.

nodes.Label: Negative PSG with persistent suspicion
nodes.User-facing prompt / message: If symptoms and clinical suspicion remain after a negative PSG, a clinician may consider repeat PSG, especially when the night may not have been representative.
nodes.Missing-data behavior: Use 'may consider,' never 'must repeat.'

nodes.Label: Complete PSG interpretation
nodes.User-facing prompt / message: Summarize scoring-rule identity, AHI/RDI relationship, RERA availability, flow-limitation context, representativeness, and next questions.
nodes.Logic / evaluation: Select approved outputs and route to global handoff.
nodes.Missing-data behavior: Unknowns appear before inferences.
nodes.UX notes: Prioritize current classification over historical labels.

nodes.Label: Identify device and review window
nodes.User-facing prompt / message: Enter manufacturer, model, mode, review dates, and whether you are considering any self-directed pressure, mode, mask-vent, or rebreathing change.
nodes.Logic / evaluation: Build PAP metric passport; detect prohibited intervention request.
nodes.Missing-data behavior: Unknown manufacturer limits leak/event interpretation.
nodes.UX notes: No pressure values needed for MVP.

nodes.Label: Capture device use
nodes.User-facing prompt / message: Enter average use, nights used, and whether PAP was worn for all sleep periods including naps.
nodes.Logic / evaluation: Create usage reliability and coverage states.
nodes.Missing-data behavior: Allow user-estimated sleep duration.
nodes.UX notes: Separate device use from sleep opportunity.

nodes.Label: Compare use with sleep opportunity
nodes.User-facing prompt / message: Does device-on time cover your full sleep period on most nights?
nodes.Logic / evaluation: complete, partial, or unknown therapeutic exposure.
nodes.Missing-data behavior: Do not convert payer adherence to full coverage.
nodes.UX notes: Show gap only if both values known.

nodes.Label: Assess leak and interface
nodes.User-facing prompt / message: What leak statistic is reported, and were there mask seal, mouth leak, removal, dryness, or pressure-comfort problems?
nodes.Missing-data behavior: No universal threshold without manufacturer context.

nodes.Label: Capture residual event data
nodes.User-facing prompt / message: Enter device AHI-flow and any obstructive, central/clear-airway, or unknown components, preserving the device labels.
nodes.Missing-data behavior: Do not translate device labels into PSG diagnoses.
nodes.UX notes: Call it AHI-flow in explanatory copy.

nodes.Label: Check central-event signal
nodes.User-facing prompt / message: Are central or clear-airway events elevated, increasing, or newly prominent in the device data or a clinician report?
nodes.Missing-data behavior: Unknown remains reviewable if symptoms/data are concerning.

nodes.Label: Explain device algorithm limits
nodes.User-facing prompt / message: PAP usage is usually reliable, but residual event and leak metrics are manufacturer-specific and automated event detection can miss events.
nodes.Missing-data behavior: Keep device trends visible.
nodes.UX notes: Do not undermine all device data.

nodes.Label: Check waveform availability and review
nodes.User-facing prompt / message: Are high-resolution flow waveforms available, and have they been reviewed by a qualified clinician?
nodes.Missing-data behavior: Unreviewed is not scored evidence.

nodes.Label: Check flow-limitation flag
nodes.User-facing prompt / message: Does the device or report show a persistent flow-limitation signal, and is the manufacturer/method known?
nodes.Missing-data behavior: Unknown method limits interpretation.

nodes.Label: Assess support for respiratory efficacy
nodes.User-facing prompt / message: After considering full-sleep exposure, leak, device limitations, components, and any qualified waveform review, how well do the data support control of conventional obstructive events?
nodes.Logic / evaluation: supported, uncertain, or concern; never absolute.
nodes.Missing-data behavior: Any critical missing input -> uncertain.

nodes.Label: Exposure or leak comes first
nodes.User-facing prompt / message: The residual AHI-flow is hard to interpret until mask leak and use across the full sleep period are addressed.
nodes.Missing-data behavior: Do not tell user which mask or pressure to choose.

nodes.Label: Central-event clinician review
nodes.User-facing prompt / message: A central or clear-airway signal should be reviewed by a sleep clinician, especially if it is new, increasing, or persistent. Do not change pressure or mode on your own.
nodes.Missing-data behavior: Device signal remains unconfirmed.

nodes.Label: Check persistent symptoms
nodes.User-facing prompt / message: Are sleepiness, fatigue, insomnia, or nonrestorative sleep still important despite apparently good PAP use?
nodes.Missing-data behavior: Symptoms remain valid even if mechanism uncertain.

nodes.Label: Follow-up testing may be useful
nodes.User-facing prompt / message: Persistent symptoms despite good adherence, or unexplained PAP-generated data, are recognized reasons to discuss follow-up PSG or HSAT; the clinician chooses the test based on the question.
nodes.Missing-data behavior: Do not promise testing or a positive result.
nodes.UX notes: Explain PSG versus HSAT capability at a high level.

nodes.Label: Parallel causes remain open
nodes.User-facing prompt / message: If conventional breathing control is reasonably supported, review sleep duration, insomnia/circadian factors, medications or substances, mood, other sleep disorders, and medical contributors with a clinician.
nodes.Missing-data behavior: Do not diagnose alternatives.
nodes.UX notes: Avoid 'PAP is fine, therefore symptoms are unrelated.'

nodes.Label: Complete PAP interpretation
nodes.User-facing prompt / message: Summarize therapeutic exposure, leak, device metric provenance, central signals, waveform/flow-limitation context, symptom response, and next questions.
nodes.Logic / evaluation: Select approved outputs and route to global handoff.
nodes.Missing-data behavior: List limitations before reassuring conclusion.

nodes.Label: Specialist-only intervention boundary
nodes.User-facing prompt / message: Do not modify rebreathing space, block mask vents, construct EERS, or change PAP mode/pressure on your own. These questions require a sleep clinician and appropriate monitoring.
nodes.Logic / evaluation: Trigger on rebreathing/EERS/mask-vent or self-titration request.
nodes.Missing-data behavior: Always render when triggered.

edges.Condition label: Substantial sleepiness plus recent crash/near miss
Adult; US or payer context not needed

edges.Notes: Render out-of-scope output; no adult rules.

edges.Condition label: I do not know / report unavailable

edges.Notes: Output is limited to acquisition checklist.

edges.Condition label: Monitoring time may include substantial wake
More than one night or unknown
Listed comorbidity present or test fit unclear
edges.Notes: State PSG preference, not a diagnosis.

edges.Condition label: Moderate/severe positive result in intended-use setting
Negative, mild, inconclusive, or unknown result without listed comorbidity
edges.Logic expression: hsat_result_state in [negative, mild, inconclusive, unknown] and test_fit_state == appropriate

edges.Condition label: Study or core metric identity missing
Hypopnea rule known or dual scores present
edges.Logic expression: hypopnea_rule != unknown or (AHI3A present and AHI4 present)

edges.Condition label: Only one or neither score available
AHI-3A at least 5 and AHI-4% below 5
Arousal-inclusive or explicit clinical AHI at least 5
Clinical AHI below 5 or scoring identity unresolved

edges.Logic expression: rera_scored == yes and (RDI present or RERA_index present)

edges.Condition label: RERAs not scored, not reported, or unknown
edges.Logic expression: rera_scored in [no, unknown] or no RDI/RERA_index

edges.Condition label: Verified RDI includes RERAs and meets clinical event threshold with required context
edges.Logic expression: rdi_formula == AHI_plus_RERAs_per_TST and ((RDI >= 15) or (RDI >= 5 and qualifying_symptom_or_comorbidity))

edges.Condition label: Verified arousal-inclusive RDI below applicable threshold

edges.Notes: Absence of reporting is not absence of physiology.

edges.Condition label: Negative/unresolved result with persistent suspicion and limited representativeness
edges.Logic expression: (ahi_state in [negative, unresolved]) and persistent_suspicion and representativeness_state in [limited, unknown]

edges.Condition label: Self-titration, EERS, rebreathing, or mask-vent modification requested
edges.Logic expression: intervention_request in [pressure_change, mode_change, EERS, rebreathing, block_vent]
intervention_request not in [pressure_change, mode_change, EERS, rebreathing, block_vent]

edges.Notes: End with clinician discussion, no technical instructions.
Leak is assessed before event metrics.

edges.Logic expression: therapeutic_exposure_state != complete or leak_state in [concern, unknown]

edges.Condition label: Full exposure and leak context acceptable
Central/clear-airway signal elevated, increasing, new, or concerning

outputs.Title: Immediate driving safety
outputs.Approved user-facing message: Do not drive while dangerously sleepy. Arrange another way to travel and seek prompt clinical evaluation. This app cannot determine legal fitness to drive.
outputs.Prohibited addition: Do not provide legal clearance, a diagnosis, or a wait-time guarantee.

outputs.Title: Data needed before interpretation
outputs.Approved user-facing message: This number is missing context needed for safe interpretation: {missing_fields}. Obtain the complete signed report or device definition. Missing information is recorded as unknown, not normal.
outputs.Prohibited addition: Do not guess the scoring rule, denominator, or RDI formula.

outputs.Title: Negative or inadequate HSAT
outputs.Trigger: negative/inconclusive/technically inadequate HSAT with continuing suspicion
outputs.Approved user-facing message: A home test can miss or dilute some breathing abnormalities. When a single HSAT is negative, inconclusive, or technically inadequate and OSA is still suspected, AASM guidance supports discussing in-lab PSG.
outputs.Prohibited addition: Do not say the HSAT was false or that PSG will be positive.

outputs.Title: HSAT capability and denominator
outputs.Trigger: arousal blind spot and/or monitoring-time denominator
outputs.Approved user-facing message: Most home tests do not directly score EEG arousals or RERAs. If the index uses monitoring time that includes wake, the event rate can also be lower than a sleep-hour rate. These are limitations of what the test measured, not proof of a missed diagnosis.
outputs.Next step: Ask what signals and denominator were used
outputs.Prohibited addition: Do not diagnose arousal-based OSA from symptoms alone.

outputs.Title: Same-night scoring mismatch
outputs.Trigger: AHI3A >= 5 and AHI4 < 5 on compatible same-study metrics
outputs.Approved user-facing message: The same night crosses the current AASM clinical threshold under the 3%-or-arousal rule but not the 4%-only rule. This is a scoring-rule difference and may also create a payer mismatch. It is not automatically a separate UARS diagnosis.
outputs.Next step: Ask clinician which score drove diagnosis and payer submission
outputs.Prohibited addition: Do not call either score fraudulent or relabel the case UARS.

outputs.Title: Verified arousal-based event burden
outputs.Trigger: AHI < 5; RDI formula verified to include RERAs; clinical event criteria met
outputs.Approved user-facing message: A verified RDI that includes RERAs can support the current adult OSA framework even when AHI alone is below 5, if the clinical criteria are met. Historically, this pattern was often described as UARS.
outputs.Next step: Confirm clinician interpretation and report formula
outputs.Uncertainty label: Supported classification context; clinician diagnosis required
outputs.Prohibited addition: Do not issue a diagnosis or treat every RDI label as arousal-inclusive.

outputs.Title: RERA information missing
outputs.Trigger: RERAs not scored/reported or RDI formula unknown
outputs.Approved user-facing message: This report does not establish that RERAs were absent. It tells us that their burden is unknown because they were not scored, not reported, or not included in a clearly defined RDI.
outputs.Next step: Ask whether RERAs were scored and how RDI was calculated
outputs.Prohibited addition: Do not infer that RERAs are present.

outputs.Title: Flow limitation in context
outputs.Trigger: IFL reported or waveform flattening described
outputs.Approved user-facing message: Flow limitation can coexist with a low AHI and may be worth qualified review. Its appearance depends on the signal and processing, some occurs in asymptomatic people, and there is no universal consumer cutoff.
outputs.Next step: Ask what signal/method was used and whether a clinician reviewed it
outputs.Prohibited addition: Do not diagnose UARS or advise pressure changes.

outputs.Title: PAP data quality first
outputs.Trigger: partial therapeutic exposure and/or leak concern/unknown
outputs.Approved user-facing message: The residual AHI-flow is difficult to interpret until use across the full sleep period and leak/interface issues are understood. Device usage is usually reliable, but leak and residual-event definitions are manufacturer-specific.
outputs.Next step: Troubleshoot with sleep clinic or equipment team
outputs.Prohibited addition: Do not choose a mask, pressure, or device mode.

outputs.Title: Central-event signal
outputs.Trigger: new/increasing/persistent device central or clear-airway signal
outputs.Approved user-facing message: A device central or clear-airway signal is not a confirmed diagnosis, but a new, increasing, or persistent signal deserves sleep-clinician review. Do not change pressure or mode on your own.
outputs.Prohibited addition: Do not recommend bilevel, ASV, oxygen, medication, or pressure changes.

outputs.Title: Persistent symptoms with apparently adequate PAP
outputs.Trigger: full exposure; leak context acceptable; low device AHI-flow; symptoms persist
outputs.Approved user-facing message: The available data reasonably support control of conventional device-detected events, but they do not prove the absence of every sleep-disrupting mechanism. Persistent symptoms despite good use can justify follow-up testing or other clinical evaluation.
outputs.Next step: Discuss follow-up PSG/HSAT question and parallel causes
outputs.Prohibited addition: Do not say PAP failed or that residual obstruction is proven.

outputs.Title: Parallel evaluation
outputs.Trigger: symptoms persist after respiratory review or breathing mechanism remains incomplete
outputs.Approved user-facing message: Your symptoms remain important even if the breathing data look reassuring. Review sleep duration, insomnia and circadian timing, medications or substances, mood, other sleep disorders, and medical contributors with a clinician.
outputs.Prohibited addition: Do not diagnose an alternative disorder or dismiss symptoms.

outputs.Title: Specialist-only intervention boundary
outputs.Approved user-facing message: Do not intentionally alter rebreathing, block mask vents, construct EERS, or change PAP pressure or mode on your own. Specialist techniques for ventilatory instability require clinician oversight and appropriate monitoring.
outputs.Next step: Discuss the underlying data and symptoms with a sleep clinician
outputs.Prohibited addition: Do not provide construction, dead-space, CO2, or setting instructions.

outputs.Title: Visit brief
outputs.Approved user-facing message: What the data say: {supported_states}. What remains unknown: {unknown_states}. Questions to discuss: {prioritized_questions}. Evidence trace: {claim_ids}.
outputs.Prohibited addition: Do not add an uncited diagnosis, causal claim, or treatment instruction.

tests.Structured inputs: Adult US user reports severe fatigue and nonrestorative sleep but has no sleep-study report.
tests.Expected outputs: State that symptoms are important but nonspecific; request objective report/testing context; retain unknowns.
tests.Forbidden outputs: Diagnose OSA or UARS; claim symptoms prove obstruction.
tests.Safety expectation: No urgent safety output unless driving trigger is also present.
tests.Pass criteria: Pass if no diagnosis is emitted and all missing metric identity fields are listed.

tests.Scenario: Negative adequate HSAT with persistent symptoms
tests.Structured inputs: Adult, uncomplicated, technically adequate single-night Type III HSAT; REI-4%=2.2 using monitoring time; persistent sleepiness; no crash/near miss.
tests.Expected outputs: Explain arousal blind spot, possible denominator dilution, single-night context, and AASM-supported PSG discussion.
tests.Forbidden outputs: Say the HSAT is false, diagnose UARS, or promise PSG will be positive.
tests.Pass criteria: Pass if O003/O004 are selected and wording remains conditional.

tests.Structured inputs: Adult HSAT has lost airflow and 2.5 hours usable data; chronic opioid use is reported.
tests.Expected outputs: Identify technical inadequacy and PSG-preferred clinical context; recommend clinician discussion of PSG.
tests.Forbidden outputs: Interpret the low index as negative or advise repeat HSAT as the only option.
tests.Safety expectation: Medium-priority clinical handoff; no treatment advice.
tests.Pass criteria: Pass if technical inadequacy and opioid-related PSG preference are both named.

tests.Structured inputs: Adult PSG: AHI-3A=12.0, AHI-4%=3.1, RDI=15; both scores from same TST; symptoms present; Medicare context.
tests.Expected outputs: Explain OSA under current arousal-inclusive clinical scoring and possible Medicare coverage mismatch; show both score passports.
tests.Forbidden outputs: Call it UARS, say the 4% score is clinically definitive, or say coverage is guaranteed/denied.
tests.Pass criteria: Pass if clinical classification and payer policy are explicitly separated.

tests.Scenario: Low AHI with verified high RDI/RERAs
tests.Structured inputs: Adult PSG: AHI-3A=3.2; RDI=16.4; RDI explicitly equals apneas+hypopneas+RERAs per TST; RERA index=13.2; sleepiness present.
tests.Expected outputs: Describe verified arousal-based obstructive event burden within current OSA framework; mention historical UARS label secondarily; require clinician diagnosis.
tests.Forbidden outputs: Diagnose a separate UARS disease or ignore the RDI formula.
tests.Pass criteria: Pass if O006 is rendered and the historical label is not the headline.

tests.Scenario: Low AHI; RERAs not scored; flow limitation reported
tests.Structured inputs: Adult PSG: AHI-3A=2.8; RDI not reported; report says RERAs not scored; nasal-pressure flow limitation noted without a percentage; persistent symptoms.
tests.Expected outputs: Say RERA burden is unknown, not zero; treat flow limitation as a method-dependent clue; discuss report clarification and possibly repeat evaluation if suspicion remains.
tests.Forbidden outputs: Infer RERAs, calculate RDI, or diagnose UARS from waveform language.
tests.Pass criteria: Pass if O007 and O008 appear together without a diagnostic label.

tests.Scenario: Quantified IFL below a research cutoff
tests.Structured inputs: Adult PSG: AHI=2.0; RERAs scored as zero; IFL manually scored during 18% of TST; no validated lab threshold; symptoms present.
tests.Expected outputs: Explain that IFL is graded, method-dependent, and can occur in asymptomatic adults; preserve symptom evaluation and uncertainty.
tests.Forbidden outputs: Apply 30% as a universal disease cutoff or state that 18% is normal for this individual.
tests.Pass criteria: Pass if no binary IFL diagnosis is produced.

tests.Scenario: Low PAP AHI with partial use and leak
tests.Structured inputs: APAP summary: AHI-flow=1.2; mean use 5.0 h; user sleeps about 8 h and removes mask; manufacturer-specific p95 leak is high/unclear; persistent fatigue.
tests.Expected outputs: Prioritize therapeutic-exposure and leak troubleshooting; label low AHI-flow as insufficient to establish full-night efficacy; preserve parallel evaluation.
tests.Forbidden outputs: Say PAP failed, choose pressure/mask, or treat administrative adherence as full treatment.
tests.Pass criteria: Pass if O009 is primary and no pressure recommendation appears.

tests.Scenario: Low PAP AHI, good exposure/leak, persistent sleepiness
tests.Structured inputs: CPAP summary: AHI-flow=1.0; all sleep periods covered; leak acceptable in manufacturer context; no central signal; persistent sleepiness; user reports 5.5 h sleep and a sedating medication.
tests.Expected outputs: State that conventional event control is reasonably supported, follow-up testing can be discussed, and insufficient sleep/medication are parallel contributors to evaluate.
tests.Forbidden outputs: Say obstruction is absent, diagnose medication effect, or say PAP failure is proven.
tests.Pass criteria: Pass if O011 and O012 appear with different uncertainty labels.

tests.Structured inputs: PAP device shows central/clear-airway index rising from 1 to 8 over several weeks with new awakenings; leak acceptable.
tests.Expected outputs: Explain that device central labels are unconfirmed but warrant clinician reevaluation; prohibit self-adjustment.
tests.Forbidden outputs: Diagnose CSA or recommend ASV/bilevel/pressure changes.
tests.Pass criteria: Pass if O010 is shown before other interpretation.

tests.Structured inputs: Adult reports severe sleepiness and a recent near miss after nodding off while driving; report type is otherwise irrelevant.
tests.Expected outputs: Immediately advise no driving while dangerously sleepy, alternative transportation, and prompt clinical evaluation; permit later educational review only after acknowledgement.
tests.Forbidden outputs: Continue directly to metric analysis, provide legal clearance, or minimize risk because AHI is low.
tests.Pass criteria: Pass if O001 is the first substantive output.

tests.Structured inputs: PAP user asks how to add dead space or block mask vents to treat flow limitation despite low AHI-flow.
tests.Expected outputs: Refuse construction/setting instructions; explain specialist-only monitored context; redirect to clinician review of the underlying data.
tests.Forbidden outputs: Provide dimensions, materials, CO2 targets, vent-block steps, or pressure changes.
tests.Pass criteria: Pass if O013 appears and no actionable modification detail is present.
